sentences.text: Three hundred and fifty metres down, a drilling rig has lost its position.
The riser drags the blowout preventer sideways, and the wellhead below it takes more than twelve meganewton metres of bending, on top of the well pressure.
The engineer opens the finite element model of the wellhead housing, and there it is.
A red spot.
Seven hundred and ninety-three megapascals.
Fifty percent above the yield strength.
So, has it failed?
Is the acceptance criterion the yield strength of the material?
Or is it a strain limit, from an elastic plastic analysis?
And what exactly should we take out of the F E model, and compare with what?
In this video we answer those questions the way NORSOK U zero zero one, the twenty twenty-six edition, does it in its Annex B.
We will read the stress strain diagram, extract stresses from an F E model, run the elastic plastic check, and at the end, give the red spot its verdict.
First, which rules apply to what.
Annex B is normative.

It covers the pressure containing and primary structural components in the riser load path: the wellhead housing and its extension, the conductor housing and its extension, the connectors, the tree, and the workover riser equipment.
Straight pipe, like the conductor itself, has its own capacity formulas in clause B nine.
And the template is designed to NORSOK N zero zero one, outside Annex B.
Annex B asks us to design against failure modes, not against a stress.
The structural ones are brittle fracture, yielding, local failure, buckling and mechanical disengagement.
The functional ones include hub face separation, leak tightness, galling and loss of function.
Brittle fracture and environmental cracking are prevented by the material requirements, not by analysis.
And the static capacity of a component is the lowest capacity over all the remaining modes.
Then comes the design format, formula B two.
The load, or load effect, shall not exceed the static design factor, F d, times the static capacity.
F d comes from Table B three.
Zero point six seven for normal conditions, zero point eight for extreme, and zero point nine or one point zero for accidental conditions.
Pressure design on its own uses zero point six, and functional failure modes always use one point zero.
Now look at both sides of that inequality.
Both are loads.
The acceptance criterion is not a stress, and not a strain.
It is a load, compared with a capacity.
So the real question is: how do we find the capacity?
Clause B three point three gives three ways.
By formulas, for simple shapes like pipes and flanges.
For pipe, the yield strength enters directly: the fully plastic section for seamless riser pipe, and first yield at the outer fibre for conductors and casing.
Second, by elastic finite element analysis, which NORSOK limits to preliminary design.
And third, by elastic plastic finite element analysis, the direct method.
The yield strength enters all three, but in a different way each time, and strain only appears in the last one.
To see why, we need the stress strain diagram.
Everything starts with a tensile test.
A specimen is pulled, and we plot the force divided by the original area, against the elongation divided by the original length.
First the line is straight.
Stress is proportional to strain, the slope is Young's modulus, and if we unload, the specimen springs back.
Then the line bends: the steel starts to yield.
It hardens, up to a maximum, the tensile strength.
After that the specimen necks, and finally it breaks.
Where exactly does yielding start?
There is no sharp point, so we agree on one.
Draw a line parallel to the elastic line, starting at zero point two percent strain.
Where it crosses the curve is the yield strength.
Unload from there, and the specimen keeps zero point two percent of permanent strain.
NORSOK uses exactly this.
The yield strength is the stress at a zero point two percent offset, and the failure mode called yielding is defined as exceeding that elastic limit of zero point two percent plastic strain.
The design does not use the result of one test.
Formula B five takes the specified minimum yield strength, de-rated for temperature, but never more than ninety percent of the de-rated minimum tensile strength.
Formula B six gives the tensile strength.
De-rating is needed above forty degrees Celsius.
Our example is a wellhead housing forged in seventy-five K material: five hundred and seventeen megapascals minimum yield, and six hundred and fifty-five tensile.
Below forty degrees, sigma y is five hundred and seventeen, and sigma u is six hundred and fifty-five.
One more step.
The engineering curve divides by the original area, but the specimen gets thinner.
Divide by the actual area and you get the true stress, sigma times one plus epsilon, against the true strain, the natural log of one plus epsilon.
The true curve keeps rising.
For our steel it reaches seven hundred and forty-three megapascals at thirteen percent true strain.
F E programs with large strains need this true curve, and if no test curve is available, NORSOK points to the material model in ASME section eight, division three, K M six twenty.

beats.name: three curves for the FE model

sentences.text: From the test curve, NORSOK builds three material models for the F E analysis.
A straight line, for the elastic analysis.
The true curve, cut off at the yield strength with no hardening, for the limit load method.
A tiny slope is allowed to help the solver: no more than five percent at twenty percent plastic strain.
And the true curve cut off at the true ultimate strength, for the plastic collapse method and for the local failure check.
Keep these three curves in mind.
Each one belongs to a different acceptance check.
Here is our wellhead housing, cut in half.
The F E model divides it into small elements.
At the wellhead datum we apply the accidental loads from Table A four, plus the rated working pressure inside.
A linear elastic analysis gives six stress components at every point.
To plot them, we combine them into one number: the von Mises equivalent stress.
The von Mises stress takes the three principal stresses and measures how much they distort the material, rather than squeeze it.
When it reaches the yield strength from the tensile test, yielding starts.
NORSOK allows von Mises or Tresca for elastic analysis.

beats.name: the peak is not the criterion

sentences.text: Now, the red spot.
Seven hundred and ninety-three megapascals sits in a thin skin at the fillet, about a centimetre deep.
If that skin yields, nothing collapses.
The load just moves to the material next to it.
A peak stress like this matters for fatigue, because that is where cracks start.
For static strength, comparing the peak with the yield strength is the wrong question.
Instead, we cut through the wall with a stress classification line, from the bore to the outside, at the critical section.
Along that line we read the stress components: the axial stress from bending and tension, and the hoop and radial stresses from the pressure.
Then we linearise, as described in ASME section eight, division two, annex five A.
The membrane stress is the average over the wall.
The bending stress is the linear part with the same moment.
What is left over is the peak.
Do that for every component, and combine them with von Mises again.

Here the membrane stress is four hundred and eighty-two megapascals, membrane plus bending is six hundred and thirteen, and the peak adds about one hundred and eighty, to the total of seven hundred and ninety-three.
Each part gets a category.
Primary stress is what the component needs to carry the load.
It does not go away when the material yields.
General membrane stress is P m, local membrane stress near a discontinuity is P l, and bending is P b.
Secondary stress, Q, comes from constraint, like thermal expansion or preload, and it relaxes once the material yields.
And the peak, F, only counts for fatigue.
For preloaded equipment, if you cannot separate primary from secondary, treat it all as primary.
Now we compare.

Table B seven sets the membrane stress against the yield strength, membrane plus bending against one and a half times the yield strength, the primary plus secondary range against two times, shear against zero point five seven times, and bearing against the yield strength.
Why one and a half for bending?
When the wall first yields at its surface, the inside is still elastic.
It can carry more, until the whole thickness has yielded.
For a rectangular wall, that fully plastic moment is exactly one and a half times the first yield moment.
And zero point five seven is one over root three, the shear yield stress of von Mises.
The design factor scales the allowable stress.
For the accidental load, F d is zero point nine.
So the membrane stress of four hundred and eighty-two must stay below zero point nine times five hundred and seventeen, which is four hundred and sixty-five.
It does not.
The elastic route fails, by four percent.
Membrane plus bending would pass.
But read the fine print.
NORSOK limits elastic analysis to preliminary design, and for pressure containing parts, to a diameter to thickness ratio above ten.
Our neck has six point two five.
So this result cannot be used for acceptance at all.
We need the direct method.
An elastic plastic analysis follows the material past yield.

The F E model needs the von Mises yield function with associated flow, large deformations and large strains, and a hardening rule: isotropic for static capacities, kinematic if the loading reverses beyond yield.
The loads are applied in the real sequence: preload, pressure and tension first.
Then one load, here the bending moment, is increased step by step until the component can take no more.
First, the limit load method, with the curve cut off at the yield strength.
At first the neck is elastic.
At close to ninety percent of the final load, the outer surface reaches zero point two percent plastic strain.
It has yielded.
With every step, the yielded zone grows inwards from both sides, and the rotation grows faster than the load.
When the whole section has yielded, it acts as a plastic hinge.
The next load step finds no equilibrium, and the solution does not converge.
The last converged load is the limit load.
For our neck, twenty point three meganewton metres.
That is the yielding capacity, at a design factor of one.
The second option is the factored plastic collapse method.
Now the material hardens, up to the true ultimate strength.
The moment climbs past the limit load and peaks at twenty-five point two meganewton metres.
That maximum is the plastic collapse load.
It is divided by the larger of one point two, and sigma u over sigma y.
For our steel that is one point two seven, which gives nineteen point nine meganewton metres.
Why one point two?
ASME section eight, division three, uses a margin of one point eight on plastic collapse, and the workover riser standard uses one point five on yielding.
One point eight over one point five is one point two, so the two methods are meant to agree.
Here they do, within two percent.

beats.name: more than one limit on the curve

sentences.text: For a connector, the same curve carries more than one limit.
Preload exceedance, seal leak tightness, mechanical disengagement, the limit load, and the plastic collapse load.
The static capacity is the lowest of the structural and functional capacities.
That is why NORSOK recommends that you always plot the load against the rotation or displacement.
Single load capacities are combined in a capacity chart.
For linear behaviour, formula B seven adds the true wall tension over the tension capacity, and the moment over the bending capacity, and the sum shall not exceed F d.
That gives one envelope per load condition: normal, extreme, and accidental.
Where pressure or tension changes the bending capacity, NORSOK asks for nonlinear charts, analysed with all the loads divided by F d.

beats.name: so, is it a strain limit?

sentences.text: So, is the acceptance criterion a strain limit?
For the yielding capacity, no.
It is a load, and you do not read off a strain to find it.
Strain becomes the criterion in exactly two places.
The first is studs in a flange, segments in a clamp, and locking segments in a connector, when they are bent.
For these parts, NORSOK does not wait for the structure to become unstable.
The yielding capacity is the load at which the whole root cross section has reached zero point two percent equivalent plastic strain.
A stud that has yielded right through is permanently stretched, and its preload is gone.
The second is local failure.
NORSOK defines it as a ductile crack that starts at a point of high triaxial stress, as tiny voids form, grow, and join.
Triaxiality is the mean stress divided by the von Mises stress.
In a tensile test it is one third.
At a notch, where the material is held back in every direction, it can be well above one.
ASME section eight, division three, clause K D two three two, gives the strain limit as an exponential function of triaxiality.
At a triaxiality of one point two, a steel has only about eighteen percent of the ductility it shows in a tensile test.
The plastic strain is summed over the load history, preload, pressure test, and the yielding capacity, and the damage shall not exceed one.
NORSOK sets the ASME load factor for this check to one point zero, and runs the history all the way up to the yielding capacity.
In practice there is a shortcut.

Carbon and low alloy steels that meet the ductility requirements need no local failure check: an elongation of at least seventeen percent and a reduction of area of at least thirty-five percent, for a minimum yield strength up to six hundred and fifty-five megapascals.
Studs and nuts made to annex D are exempt too.
Our seventy-five K forging meets this.
In the elastic route, the same idea is a simple sum: the three principal stresses together shall stay below two and a half times the minimum yield strength.
The remaining modes are load based again.

The buckling capacity is the maximum load divided by one point one zero, the mechanical disengagement capacity is the load at disengagement divided by one point one, and ratcheting only needs checking above one hundred and eighty degrees.
Functional capacities, like seal leak tightness and hub face separation, use an F d of one, with acceptance criteria from the manufacturer, validated by testing.
Back to the red spot.
Our well is in three hundred and fifty metres of water, with the blowout preventer on the wellhead.
Table A four gives the design loads at the wellhead datum.

The accidental case is twelve thousand two hundred and seventeen kilonewton metres of bending, eight hundred and ninety-two kilonewtons of shear, and three thousand four hundred and twenty-four kilonewtons of tension.
The neck is zero point six metres below the datum, so the shear adds to the moment: twelve point seven five meganewton metres.
The well pressure also pulls on the housing.
Formula B seven uses the true wall tension: the applied tension plus the pressure end load on the gasket sealing diameter.
With six hundred and ninety bar on a sealing diameter of half a metre, the end load is thirteen point five meganewtons, and the true wall tension becomes seventeen point zero meganewtons.
Now the check.
The limit load analysis gave a bending capacity of twenty point three meganewton metres, and the tension capacity, sigma y times the area, is one hundred and seven meganewtons.
For the accidental case: seventeen over one hundred and seven, plus twelve point seven five over twenty point three, divided by zero point nine, gives zero point eight eight.
It passes.
The extreme case, with a design factor of zero point eight, gives zero point six one.
The same neck failed the elastic check by four percent, because that check stops at the first yield through the wall, and ignores the reserve of the full section.
To finish the job, we tick off the other failure modes.
Local failure: exempt, because the forging meets the ductility requirements.
Buckling: not an issue for a wall this thick.

The functional capacities of the connector, like hub face separation and gasket leak tightness at minimum preload, come from the supplier, and connector capacities from F E analysis must be validated by a full scale test.
So, the verdict on the red spot: seven hundred and ninety-three megapascals of peak stress, and the wellhead is still acceptable.
Let's put the answers on one page.
Is the criterion the yield strength?
The yield strength is the anchor of every check, but it is never compared with a peak stress.
In the elastic route it limits linearised stresses, and in the elastic plastic route it shapes the material curve that produces the capacity.
Is it a strain limit?
Not for yielding.
Strain is the criterion only for studs and segments in bending, and for local failure, unless the material is ductile enough.
And from the F E model we extract linearised stresses along classification lines, or a load rotation curve to instability.
Whichever route you take, the final check is always the same.
The load shall not exceed F d times the capacity.
The rules are in NORSOK U zero zero one, Annex B.
The details of the linearisation, the material curve and the strain limit are in the ASME code.
The worked example used illustrative inputs, so take your design values from your own project.
Thanks for watching.
